nameStory: This grasshopper gets its name from its distinctive olive-green coloration that helps it blend perfectly into the marshy vegetation of swamps and wetlands. The name 'swamp grasshopper' tells you exactly where to look for this moisture-loving insect, while 'olive-green' describes the muted, earthy color that makes it a master of camouflage among wet grasses and sedges.
description: The Olive-green Swamp Grasshopper is a medium-sized grasshopper with a muted olive-green to brownish coloration that makes it blend seamlessly into wetland vegetation. Like other short-horned grasshoppers, it has relatively short antennae compared to katydids and crickets. Adults typically measure about an inch to inch and a half in length. This moisture-loving grasshopper is specially adapted for life in wet, marshy environments where many other grasshoppers can't survive.

idTips.label: Olive-green coloration
idTips.description: The body has a distinctive muted olive-green to brownish-green color that looks almost mossy, helping it disappear among wet marsh grasses and sedges

idTips.label: Short antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are noticeably shorter than the body length, feeling thick and sturdy when observed up close - a key feature of short-horned grasshoppers

idTips.label: Wetland habitat
idTips.description: Always found in or very close to wet areas - if you're not near water or soggy ground, you're probably looking at a different grasshopper species

idTips.label: Powerful hind legs
idTips.description: Large, muscular jumping legs with a slightly sticky feel when handled, adapted for gripping wet vegetation and launching from muddy surfaces

idTips.label: Moist body texture
idTips.description: Body feels slightly more humid and less dry than typical grasshoppers, an adaptation to its wetland lifestyle

habitat: Look for Olive-green Swamp Grasshoppers in freshwater marshes, swamp edges, wet meadows, and boggy areas throughout New England's lowlands. They prefer areas with standing water or saturated soil, often hiding among cattails, sedges, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll rarely find them far from water sources like ponds, slow streams, or seasonal wetlands.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs are developing in the moist soil and plant debris of wetland areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively feeding on marsh grasses and beginning to mate in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active through early fall, with females laying eggs in wet soil before the first hard frosts end their season.
seasonality.winter: Only eggs survive the winter, tucked safely in the moist soil and decomposing vegetation of marshes and swamps.

funFact: These grasshoppers can actually swim short distances and don't panic when they fall into water - instead, they use their powerful legs to paddle to safety, making them one of the few grasshoppers that are truly aquatic-adapted!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other green grasshoppers, but remember the habitat rule: if it's not in or right next to a wetland, it's probably a different species. The olive-green color is more muted and 'muddy' looking than the bright green of meadow grasshoppers.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'clavuligera' means 'club-bearing,' likely referring to the shape of certain body parts, though this detail isn't obvious to casual observers. Focus on the habitat and color for field identification.
compareHints: Since this is the only swamp grasshopper species in our region, compare it to other wetland-dwelling Orthoptera like the Short-winged Meadow Katydid, which has much longer antennae. Among grasshoppers, most other green species prefer drier habitats and have brighter, more vibrant green coloration rather than the muted olive tones of this wetland specialist.
